writing.explanation:
Build a_prefix=[4,1] and b_prefix=[5,6,1] as separate nodes, then attach both to shared=[8,4,5]. Pointer identities first agree at 8. Equal-valued private prefixes remain distinct; an empty shared tail means no intersection.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Parse a_prefix, b_prefix and shared integer arrays. Build separate prefix nodes and attach both to the same shared tail. Return the first shared node value, or none when shared is empty. Equal values in separate prefixes do not identify shared nodes. The visible fixture is `a_prefix=[4,1]; b_prefix=[5,6,1]; shared=[8,4,5]` and its example result is `8`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Pointer-Switch Intersection when it asks for shared-tail intersection without lengths. Here the concrete task is: Parse a_prefix, b_prefix and shared integer arrays. Build separate prefix nodes and attach both to the same shared tail. Return the first shared node value, or none when shared is empty. Equal values in separate prefixes do not identify shared nodes. The visible input `a_prefix=[4,1]; b_prefix=[5,6,1]; shared=[8,4,5]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Look for tasks where node identity or one-way traversal matters. An indexed vector solution can hide the pointer constraint rather than solve it. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Switch each pointer to the other head so both traverse equal combined distance. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A list algorithm changes relationships between nodes, not just values. Draw the next pointers before and after each mutation. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n+m) time · O(1) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `8` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Check an empty list, one node, a head or tail change, and cycles when the problem allows them. Rust ownership makes linked structures explicit: use the provided node type, take links carefully, and preserve access to the remaining chain. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
